strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: no prior TTA method exists for vision-language object detectors (VLODs), and the paper carefully motivates why classification-style TTA (entropy minimization, prompt averaging) transfers poorly to detection due to confirmation bias and lack of proposal-structure awareness.

The two proposed components (IoU-weighted entropy minimization and image-conditioned prompt selection) are simple, lightweight, and well-motivated with clear illustrative examples (Figs. 1-2) showing concrete failure modes they address.

Extensive empirical evaluation: 6+ datasets/benchmarks (stylized domains, driving scenes, low-light, PASCAL-C, COCO-C), 15 corruption types across 5 severities, two architecturally different detectors (CNN-based YOLO-World and transformer-based Grounding DINO), and multiple backbone sizes (YW-L, GD-B), totaling many test scenarios.

Thorough ablation studies covering IoU threshold, cluster exponent, fusion coefficient, prompt-selection fraction, adapter placement per module, batch size, augmentation count, and prompt-generation strategy, which supports reproducibility and gives insight into the mechanism of the method.
Reasonable baselines adapted from VLM TTA literature (TPT, VPT, DPE) and a fair Adapter+TENT baseline, allowing isolation of the contribution of IWE/IPS beyond simply using adapters.
Additional analyses such as computational overhead/FPS comparison, effect of pre-adaptation fine-tuning, and qualitative visualizations strengthen the completeness of the empirical study.
A simple theoretical remark (cosine-Euclidean equivalence) is included, and the paper is generally clearly written with a coherent narrative connecting motivation, method, and results.
weaknesses: Gains are inconsistent and sometimes marginal in challenging domains (e.g., driving scenes with small, low-overlap objects), and the paper's own conclusion admits IWE underperforms in such settings, which somewhat limits the claimed generality of the method.

On COCO-C (Tables 8-10), standard entropy-based Adapter/TENT baseline occasionally outperforms VLOD-TTA on specific corruptions, indicating the proposed IWE objective does not uniformly dominate simpler baselines, particularly for the harder 80-class setting.

Adapter placement differs per detector (vision/neck adapters for YW vs. text-encoder-only for GD), determined empirically through ablation on the same style-shift datasets used for the main benchmark; this raises a mild concern about hyperparameter/architecture-choice overfitting to the evaluation suite rather than a principled a priori design choice.

The prompt pool used for IPS is generated by GPT without dataset-specific information, but its quality/diversity is not controlled for or compared against a wider variety of automatically generated pools; the reported gains from IPS could be sensitive to the particular prompt set chosen (dataset-specific prompts give notably larger gains, suggesting some sensitivity).

The method requires single-step gradient adaptation per image (backward pass), and although FPS is reported, the throughput drop relative to ZS (89→20 FPS on YW) is substantial, which may limit applicability in real-time detection settings central to the motivating driving/AR use cases.

Comparisons are restricted to VLM-style TTA baselines adapted to detection; no comparison is made to detection-native TTA methods (e.g., Chen et al. 2023, Yoo et al. 2023, Cao et al. 2025) discussed in related work, even though these are specifically designed for object detectors, leaving open whether VLOD-TTA's advantage stems mainly from being detection-aware versus VLM-style baselines being poorly suited by design.
No code/artifact link is provided in the submission (placeholder only), which affects immediate reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameter reporting in the appendix.

strengths: Addresses a clearly identified gap: no prior TTA method exists for vision-language object detectors, and the paper is explicit that adapting classification-oriented TTA (entropy minimization, prompt tuning, cache-based methods) to detection is non-trivial due to the presence of many proposals coupled with localization.

The two proposed components (IoU-weighted entropy minimization and image-conditioned prompt selection) are well motivated with clear illustrative failure cases (Figs. 1-2) showing why naive entropy minimization and prompt averaging fail for VLODs.

Extensive empirical evaluation: 6 mainstream detection datasets plus PASCAL-C/COCO-C with 15 corruption types across 5 severities, on two structurally different VLODs (CNN-based YOLO-World and transformer-based Grounding DINO), totaling many distinct test scenarios.

Strong set of adapted baselines (TPT, VPT, DPE, Adapter/TENT) gives a fair comparison point since no existing VLOD-specific TTA baseline exists, and the method consistently outperforms them across nearly all settings.

Thorough ablation studies covering IoU threshold, cluster exponent, fusion coefficient, number of selected prompts, adapter placement per module, batch size, number of augmentations, backbone size, and pre-adaptation fine-tuning, which supports robustness of the design choices.
Complexity/efficiency analysis (FPS, trainable parameters) demonstrates the method's practicality relative to alternatives like TPT/VPT/DPE and full fine-tuning.
Reasonable theoretical grounding (cosine-Euclidean equivalence proposition) and qualitative visualizations connecting the mechanism (dense cluster weighting) to observed improvements.

Honest limitation discussion, e.g., IWE underperforming in scenes with many tiny, low-overlap objects (Cityscapes/BDD100K), and clear statement about why dataset-specific prompts were avoided despite giving larger gains.
weaknesses: Absolute gains are often modest, particularly for driving scenes (Cityscapes, BDD100K) and at high corruption severities on COCO-C, where the standard Adapter/TENT baseline sometimes matches or exceeds VLOD-TTA on specific corruptions, somewhat diluting the strength of the central claims.

IWE weighting proposals by connected-component size in an IoU graph is a relatively incremental technical contribution built on existing entropy minimization and NMS-adjacent ideas rather than a fundamentally new detection-adaptation paradigm.

No direct comparison to existing TTA-for-object-detection methods (e.g., Chen et al. 2023, Cao et al. 2025, Ruan & Tang 2024) even in an adapted/simplified form; the paper only compares to classification-style TTA baselines re-purposed for detection, leaving open how VLOD-TTA compares to detection-specific (non-VLM) TTA approaches.

Several hyperparameters (θ, γ, λ, ρ, M) show dataset-dependent optimal values (Fig. 6), and while the paper argues for a stable range, in a fully realistic online TTA setting without access to validation data this tuning is a practical limitation not fully addressed.

Reliance on GPT-generated prompt pools introduces a dependency on an external generative model whose exact output (and thus reproducibility) may vary across GPT versions/model updates; the prompt pool itself is not clearly frozen/released for exact reproducibility.

Results are reported without variance/confidence intervals across multiple runs or seeds, making it harder to assess the statistical robustness of the reported improvements, especially where margins over the Adapter baseline are small (e.g., driving scenes).
The abstract states 'Code:' with no actual link provided in the manuscript text, leaving reproducibility contingent on future release.

strengths: Addresses a clearly identified gap: TTA for vision-language object detectors, where only one prior specialized method (TTAOD-F) exists and it is costly (teacher-student, extra forward passes).

The two proposed components (IoU-weighted entropy minimization and image-conditioned prompt selection) are simple, well-motivated with clear qualitative illustrations (Figs. 1-2), and target specific, identifiable failure modes of naive entropy minimization and prompt averaging in the detection setting.

Extensive empirical validation across a wide range of shift types (style/texture, driving domains, low-light, 15 common corruptions on two datasets) and two structurally different VLODs (CNN-based YOLO-World and transformer-based Grounding DINO), totaling many test scenarios as claimed.

Thorough ablations: component-wise contribution (Table 3), adapter vs. batch-norm parameter choice, prompt averaging vs. selection, prompt-generation strategy, adapter placement, hyperparameter sensitivity (θ, γ, M, λ, ρ), batch size, augmentation count, and effect of pre-adaptation fine-tuning.

Direct efficiency and accuracy comparison with the only prior VLOD-TTA baseline (TTAOD-F), showing comparable or better accuracy with substantially fewer tuned/total parameters, lower memory, and lower latency.

Commendable transparency in reporting and analyzing a failure case (Cityscapes), diagnosing the causes (rider/person label overlap, small objects at low resolution) with a dedicated ablation rather than hiding the weaker result.

Additional generalization checks: backbone scaling (YW-L, GD-B) and a specialized domain (underwater Aquarium dataset), plus a theoretical note (cosine-Euclidean equivalence) motivating the compatibility score in IPS.
weaknesses: The adaptation is strictly single-image / single-step with parameters reset after each prediction, which is less a form of "online adaptation accumulating knowledge over a stream" and more a per-sample self-refinement; the practical benefit versus overhead trade-off in a true streaming/continual deployment scenario is not explored.

IWE's benefit is explicitly shown to degrade when proposal overlap is sparse (small objects, Cityscapes at low resolution), and the fix (higher input resolution) trades off inference cost/latency not fully quantified in the main comparison.

The TTAOD-F comparison is conducted only on COCO-C with Grounding DINO; a broader comparison (e.g., on the stylized/domain datasets or with YOLO-World) would strengthen the claim of consistent superiority over the sole prior method.

Some hyperparameters (γ, θ, ρ, λ, M) require per-architecture and somewhat dataset-sensitive tuning (e.g., different λ for YW vs GD), which could limit plug-and-play applicability despite the paper's efficiency claims; the sensitivity plots show non-trivial dataset dependence even if described as "stable."
Only two VLOD architectures (YOLO-World and Grounding DINO, plus their L/B variants) are evaluated; generalization to other open-vocabulary detector families is untested.

The main paper's efficiency comparison (Table 7) is reported only for YOLO-World; a similarly detailed cost comparison against all baselines for Grounding DINO would make the efficiency claims more complete.

Prompt pool generation relies on GPT-generated prompts (16 per class); reproducibility depends on this external, potentially non-deterministic prompt source, and sensitivity to prompt pool size/quality beyond the tested range is not deeply explored.
